title: A Journey of Trade
subtitle: Caravan Commerce, Integrity in Busra, and the Trust of Khadijah
summary: The economic framework of pre-Islamic Arabia and the seasonal caravans, the regional trade fairs of the Hijaz, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid's commercial enterprise, Muhammad's journey with her merchandise to Syria alongside Maysarah, his honest trading in Busra, and the profitable return.

sections.text: The Caravan Economy of Ancient Arabia

Set within a barren valley devoid of agriculture, orchards, or flowing rivers, Makkah owed its survival and prosperity to its unique dual status: as the sacred sanctuary (Haram) of the Kaaba, and as the preeminent commercial crossroads of western Arabia. The merchant clans of Quraysh organized two massive seasonal trade expeditions annually, immortalized in the Holy Quran in Surah Quraysh: the winter journey southward to the spice, perfume, and incense markets of Yemen, and the summer journey northward to the grain, oil, and textile markets of Byzantine Syria and Palestine.

These expeditions required extensive capital investment, meticulous logistical coordination, and absolute trust among business partners. Hundreds of pack camels laden with tanned leather, raw wool, silver ingots, and precious frankincense traversed treacherous desert routes for weeks at a time. The commercial agreements known as the 'Ilaf,' negotiated generations earlier by Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf with regional Bedouin tribes, guaranteed safe passage through otherwise lawless territories, making Makkan caravans the essential lifeblood of regional commerce.

"For the accustomed security of the Quraysh — Their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer — Let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear." — Surah Quraysh (106:1–4)

In addition to these international expeditions, Makkah served as the coordinator of great seasonal trade fairs across the Hijaz—most notably the renowned markets of 'Ukaz, Majannah, and Dhu al-Majaz. At these vibrant assemblies, held during the Sacred Months when tribal warfare was strictly suspended, merchants exchanged commodities while poets competed in celebrated oratorical contests. Makkah's commercial prominence was therefore inseparable from its reputation for order, contractual agreements, and the neutrality of its sacred territory.
Khadijah bint Khuwaylid and Her Commercial Enterprise

Among the most respected merchants in Makkah was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad, a woman of noble lineage, sound judgement and considerable wealth. Ibn Sa'd reports that her caravan could equal the caravans of the rest of Quraysh combined. Ibn Ishaq relates that she would hire men to trade with her capital in return for a share of the profit.

Success in this system depended on the honesty and competence of the agent. Ibn Ishaq relates that when Khadijah learned of Muhammad's truthfulness, trustworthiness and noble character, she sent to him offering to have him take her merchandise to Syria, giving him more than she used to give other merchants.

A report in Ibn Sa'd's Tabaqat has Abu Talib encourage his nephew to accept, saying: 'This is a provision that God has brought to you.' Muhammad agreed and set out with Khadijah's goods, accompanied by her servant Maysarah.
Merchant caravans laden with leather, perfumes, and textiles winding through the rocky passes of the northern Hijaz.
The Journey Along Ancient Trade Routes
The caravan travelled north along the trade road from the Hijaz towards Syria, a journey of several weeks through the desert.

Upon reaching the flourishing market center of Busra in southern Syria, then a principal commercial threshold of the Byzantine Empire, the merchants pitched their camp. The markets of Busra were cosmopolitan, filled with Greek-speaking imperial administrators, Roman merchants, Syrian Christian clergy, and Arab traders from across the peninsula.
Ethical Dealings in the Markets of Busra

In the markets of Busra, Muhammad sold the goods he had brought and bought others. A report collected by Ibn Sa'd relates that a man disputed with him over a sale and asked him to swear by al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and that he replied: 'I have never sworn by them.'
Ibn Ishaq relates that Maysarah observed him throughout the journey and later told Khadijah what he had seen of his conduct.
The ancient trading markets of the Levant where merchants from across Arabia gathered.
Return to Makkah and Successful Accounting

Having sold his goods and bought what was in demand in the Hijaz, Muhammad returned with the caravan to Makkah and handed Khadijah her merchandise and her money. The sources report that the venture was profitable, more so than her earlier ones.
Beyond the profit, Khadijah listened to Maysarah's account of the journey. The biographers present this as the beginning of the esteem that led her to propose marriage to Muhammad.
For the biographers, the Syrian journey showed in practice the honesty that had already earned Muhammad the name Al-Amin.
